title: Why the Sea Has Tides
summary: How the Moon's gravity, with help from the Sun and Earth's spin, makes the sea rise and fall each day, why some tides are bigger than others, and how tides matter to people.
poll: The Moon affects life on Earth every day.

versions.title: Why the Sea Moves Up and Down
versions.text:
Sit on the shore. The sea comes up the sand. Then it goes back. This is a tide.

Most beaches get two high tides and two low tides each day.

What makes tides? The Moon! Its pull is called gravity. It tugs on the sea. The sea heaps up in a bulge. One bulge is on the side near the Moon. One more bulge is on the far side.

The Earth spins once a day. A beach spins into a bulge. That is high tide. Then it spins out. That is low tide.

The Sun pulls, too. But it is far off. So its pull on tides is less than half as strong. When the Sun and Moon line up, tides are big. These are spring tides. When they do not line up, tides are small. These are neap tides.

In Canada, a bay has tides as tall as a house! On the Red Sea shore of Saudi Arabia, tides are small.

At low tide, you can find crabs in rock pools. Ships check the tides. Tides can even make power.

versions.title: Why the Sea Has Tides
versions.text:
Sit on the shore at the beach for a few hours. Little by little, the sea creeps up the sand. Later, it slowly slides back again. This rise and fall of the sea is called a tide.

When the water is at its highest, it is high tide. When it is at its lowest, it is low tide. Most beaches have two high tides and two low tides every day.

What causes tides? The answer is the Moon. The Moon has a pulling force called gravity. Its gravity tugs on the oceans. The water piles up in a bulge on the side of the Earth that faces the Moon. A second bulge forms on the far side of the Earth.

The Earth spins all the way around once a day. As it spins, each beach moves into a bulge and then out again. Inside a bulge, it is high tide. Between the bulges, it is low tide.

The Sun pulls on the oceans, too. But the Sun is very far away. Its pull on the tides is less than half as strong as the Moon's. When the Sun and Moon line up, their pulls add together. Then tides are very big. These are called spring tides. When the Sun and Moon pull in different directions, tides are small. These are called neap tides.

Tides are not the same everywhere. In a bay in Canada, the sea can rise as high as a five-story building! On Saudi Arabia's Red Sea shore, tides are small.

Tides are useful. At low tide, you can find crabs and snails in rock pools. Ships and fishing boats check the tide times. Tides can even be used to make electricity.

If you sit on the shore at the beach for a few hours, you will notice something. Little by little, the sea creeps up the sand. Later, it slowly slides back again. This regular rise and fall of the sea is called a tide.

When the water reaches its highest point, it is high tide. When it reaches its lowest point, it is low tide. Most beaches have two high tides and two low tides every day.

What causes tides? The main cause is the Moon. Like every object in space, the Moon has a pulling force called gravity. The Moon's gravity tugs on the oceans. It makes the water pile up in a bulge on the side of the Earth that faces the Moon. A second bulge forms on the opposite side of the Earth.

The Earth spins all the way around once a day. As it turns, each beach passes into a bulge and then out again. Inside a bulge, it is high tide. Between the two bulges, it is low tide.

The Sun pulls on the oceans, too. But the Sun is so far away that its pull on the tides is less than half as strong as the Moon's. When the Sun and Moon line up, their pulls work together. This makes extra-large tides called spring tides. When the Sun and Moon pull in different directions, the tides are smaller. These are called neap tides.

Tides are not the same everywhere. In one bay in Canada, the sea can rise as high as a five-story building! On Saudi Arabia's Red Sea shore, tides are usually small.

Tides matter to people. At low tide, you can find crabs and snails in rock pools. Ships and fishing boats check tide times before they sail. Tides can even be used to make electricity.

versions.title: Why the Sea Has Tides
versions.text:
Spend a whole day on the shore, and you will see the sea change. In the morning, the waves may reach far up the beach. By lunchtime, the water may have pulled back, leaving wet sand behind. This regular rise and fall of the sea is called a tide, and most shores have two high tides and two low tides every day.

The main cause of tides is the Moon. The Moon has gravity, a force that pulls objects toward it. Its gravity tugs on the oceans and makes the water pile up in a bulge on the side of the Earth facing the Moon. A second bulge forms on the opposite side of the Earth.

Meanwhile, the Earth spins once a day, so each shore passes through both bulges. When a beach is inside a bulge, it has high tide, and when it is between the bulges, it has low tide.

The Sun pulls on the oceans, too. Because the Sun is so distant, its effect on tides is less than half as strong as the Moon's. When the Sun, Moon, and Earth are aligned in a straight line, their pulls combine, which creates extra-large tides called spring tides. When the Sun and Moon pull at right angles, the tides are weaker, and these are called neap tides.

The difference between high and low tide is called the tidal range, and it changes from place to place. In the Bay of Fundy in Canada, the range can reach about 16 meters. On Saudi Arabia's Red Sea coast, the range is usually less than one meter.

Because scientists understand these patterns, they can predict tides years ahead. Sailors use tide tables to know when a ship can safely enter a harbor. At low tide, families explore rock pools full of crabs and snails. Some countries even use moving tides to make electricity.

If you spend an entire day on the shore, you will notice that the sea refuses to remain in one place. In the morning, the waves may stretch far up the beach, but by lunchtime the water may have retreated, exposing a wide strip of glistening sand. This regular rise and fall of sea level is called a tide, and most coastlines experience two high tides and two low tides every day.

The primary cause of tides is the Moon. Every object with mass exerts gravity, an invisible force of attraction, and the Moon's gravitational pull tugs on Earth's oceans, causing water to accumulate in a bulge on the side of the planet facing the Moon. A second bulge simultaneously forms on the opposite side, because the Moon pulls the far ocean more weakly than it pulls the solid Earth, so that water is effectively left behind.

Meanwhile, Earth rotates once every day, carrying each shore through both bulges. When a beach is located inside a bulge, it experiences high tide, and when it is positioned between them, it experiences low tide.

The Sun also attracts the oceans, but because it is so distant, its influence on tides is less than half as strong as the Moon's. During the new moon and full moon phases, the Sun, Moon, and Earth are aligned, and their pulls combine to produce extra-large spring tides. During the quarter-moon phases, the Sun and Moon pull in perpendicular directions, at right angles to each other, producing weaker neap tides.

The difference between high and low tide, called the tidal range, varies enormously from one location to another. In Canada's Bay of Fundy, the range can reach approximately 16 meters, whereas along Saudi Arabia's Red Sea coast it is usually less than one meter.

Because scientists understand these patterns, they can predict tides years in advance, which makes tide tables essential for navigation. Captains consult them to determine when a ship can safely enter a harbor. At low tide, families explore rock pools teeming with crabs and snails, and some countries even harness tidal currents as a renewable source of electricity.

versions.text:
Anyone who spends an entire day on the shore will notice that the sea refuses to remain in one place. In the morning, the waves may stretch far up the beach, yet by lunchtime the water may have retreated considerably, exposing a broad strip of glistening sand. This regular rise and fall of sea level is called a tide, and most coastlines experience two high tides and two low tides every day.

The primary cause of tides is the Moon. Every object with mass exerts gravity, an invisible force of attraction, and the Moon's gravitational pull tugs on Earth's oceans, causing water to accumulate in a bulge on the side of the planet facing the Moon. A second bulge simultaneously develops on the opposite side, because the Moon attracts that distant ocean more weakly than it attracts the solid Earth, so the water is effectively left behind.

Meanwhile, Earth rotates once every day, carrying each coastline through both bulges in turn. When a beach is located inside a bulge, it experiences high tide, and when it is positioned between them, it experiences low tide.

The Sun also attracts the oceans, but because it is extraordinarily distant, its influence on tides is less than half as powerful as the Moon's. During the new moon and full moon phases, the Sun, Moon, and Earth are aligned, and their combined pull produces exceptionally large spring tides. During the quarter-moon phases, however, the Sun and Moon pull in perpendicular directions, at right angles to each other, generating comparatively weak neap tides.

The difference between high and low tide, known as the tidal range, varies enormously from one location to another, depending partly on the shape of the coastline. In Canada's Bay of Fundy, the range can reach approximately 16 meters, whereas along Saudi Arabia's Red Sea coast it is typically less than one meter.

Because scientists thoroughly understand these patterns, they can predict tides years in advance, which makes tide tables essential for safe navigation. Captains consult them to determine precisely when a vessel can enter a shallow harbor. At low tide, families explore rock pools teeming with crabs and snails, and several countries even harness tidal currents as a renewable source of electricity.

versions.text:
Anyone who spends an entire day on the shore will observe that the sea refuses to remain stationary. In the morning, the waves may stretch far up the beach, yet by midday the water may have retreated considerably, exposing a broad expanse of glistening sand. This regular rise and fall of sea level is called a tide, and the majority of coastlines experience two high tides and two low tides every day.

The primary cause of tides is the Moon. Every object possessing mass exerts gravity, an invisible force of attraction, and the Moon's gravitational pull tugs persistently on Earth's oceans, causing water to accumulate in a bulge on the side of the planet facing the Moon. A second bulge simultaneously develops on the opposite side, because the Moon attracts that distant ocean more weakly than it attracts the solid Earth, so the water is effectively left behind.

Meanwhile, Earth rotates once every day, carrying each coastline through both bulges in succession, so when a beach is located within a bulge, it experiences high tide, and when it is positioned between them, it experiences low tide.

The Sun also attracts the oceans, but because it is extraordinarily distant, its influence on tides is less than half as powerful as the Moon's. During the new moon and full moon phases, the Sun, Moon, and Earth are aligned, and their combined attraction produces exceptionally large spring tides. During the quarter-moon phases, however, the Sun and Moon pull in perpendicular directions, at right angles to each other, generating comparatively modest neap tides.

The difference between high and low tide, known as the tidal range, varies enormously from one location to another, depending partly on the geography of the coastline and the shape of the ocean floor. In Canada's Bay of Fundy, the range can reach approximately 16 meters, whereas along Saudi Arabia's Red Sea coast it is typically less than one meter.

Because oceanographers thoroughly understand these astronomical patterns, they can predict tides years in advance, which makes tide tables indispensable for safe navigation. Captains consult them to determine precisely when a heavily loaded vessel can enter a shallow harbor. At low tide, families investigate rock pools teeming with crabs and snails, and several countries even harness tidal currents as a renewable source of electricity.

versions.title: Why the Sea Has Tides
versions.text:
Anyone who spends an entire day on the shore will observe that the sea stubbornly refuses to remain stationary: in the morning, the waves may stretch far up the beach, yet by midday the water may have retreated considerably, exposing a broad expanse of glistening sand. This regular, predictable, perpetual rise and fall of sea level is called a tide, and the overwhelming majority of coastlines experience two high tides and two low tides every day.

The primary cause of tides is the Moon. Every object possessing mass exerts gravity, an invisible force of attraction, and the Moon's gravitational influence tugs persistently on Earth's oceans, causing water to accumulate in a bulge on the side of the planet facing the Moon. A second bulge simultaneously develops on the opposite side, because the Moon attracts that distant ocean more weakly than it attracts the solid Earth, with the consequence that the water is effectively left behind.

Meanwhile, Earth rotates once every day, transporting each coastline through both bulges in succession. Whenever a beach is located within a bulge, it experiences high tide, and whenever it is positioned between them, it experiences low tide.

The Sun also attracts the oceans, but because it is extraordinarily distant, its influence on tides is less than half as powerful as the Moon's. During the new moon and full moon phases, the Sun, Moon, and Earth are aligned, and their combined attraction generates exceptionally large spring tides, whereas during the quarter-moon phases the Sun and Moon pull in perpendicular directions, at right angles to each other, producing comparatively modest neap tides.

The difference between high and low tide, known as the tidal range, varies enormously from one location to another, depending substantially on the geography of the coastline and the configuration of the ocean floor. In Canada's Bay of Fundy, the range can reach approximately 16 meters, whereas along Saudi Arabia's Red Sea coast it is typically less than one meter.

Because oceanographers comprehensively understand these astronomical patterns, they can predict tides years in advance, which makes tide tables indispensable for safe navigation. Captains consult them to determine precisely when a heavily loaded commercial vessel can enter a shallow harbor. At low tide, families investigate rock pools teeming with crabs and snails, and several countries even harness tidal currents as a renewable, nonpolluting source of electricity.

keyWords.definition: able to be used again and again because nature keeps replacing it
keyWords.example: Sunlight is a renewable source of energy for many homes.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?
options: Tidal power will soon replace every other source of electricity in the world, including sunlight and wind.
Tides result mainly from the Moon's gravity, shaped by the Sun and Earth's rotation, and they matter to people.
The Bay of Fundy has the largest tides on Earth.
The Sun's gravity has no effect on the oceans.
questions.why: The article explains the causes of tides and how people use tide knowledge for navigation, exploring and electricity.

wrong.A: The article says some countries use tides for electricity, not that it will replace all sources.
wrong.C: The Bay of Fundy is an example, and the article does not call it the largest.
wrong.D: The article says the Sun does affect tides, just less than the Moon.

questions.stem: During which moon phases do spring tides occur?
options: Only during a lunar eclipse
The two quarter-moon phases
Only during the spring season
The new moon and full moon phases
questions.why: The article says that during the new moon and full moon phases, the Sun, Moon and Earth are aligned, producing spring tides.

wrong.C: Spring tides have nothing to do with the season.

questions.stem: Why does a second bulge form on the side of Earth facing away from the Moon?
options: The Moon pulls that far ocean more weakly than the solid Earth, so the water is left behind.
The Sun pushes the water to that side.
Winds pile the water there each night.
Earth's fast spin flings all of the ocean water out to one side of the planet.
questions.why: The article explains the second bulge forms because the Moon attracts the distant ocean more weakly than the solid Earth.

wrong.B: The Sun attracts water; it does not push it.
wrong.C: Wind is not given as a cause.
wrong.D: Earth's spin carries shores through the bulges; it does not create the second bulge.

questions.stem: How does the Sun's influence on tides compare with the Moon's?
options: It is about twice as strong.
It is exactly the same.
It is less than half as strong.
It is a hundred times stronger.
questions.why: The article states that because the Sun is so distant, its influence is less than half as strong as the Moon's.

wrong.A: The Sun's effect is weaker, not stronger.
wrong.D: This reverses what the article says.

questions.stem: "The Sun and Moon pull in perpendicular directions, at right angles to each other." What does perpendicular mean?
options: Facing opposite ways
At right angles
Parallel
Circular
questions.why: The sentence itself explains perpendicular with the phrase "at right angles to each other."

wrong.A: Opposite directions would be a straight line, not a right angle.
wrong.C: Parallel lines never meet; perpendicular lines meet at a corner.
wrong.D: Circular describes a curve, not a direction.

questions.stem: Why can tidal currents be called a renewable source of electricity?
options: Because they are much cheaper than every other kind of energy people use
Because they work only in the Bay of Fundy
Because they are powered by burning fuel
Because the Moon and Earth keep making new tides every day
questions.why: Tides return every day as long as the Moon pulls and Earth rotates, so the energy is constantly replaced.

wrong.A: The article does not compare costs.
wrong.B: The article says several countries use tidal currents.
wrong.C: Tides are driven by gravity, not burning fuel.

questions.stem: A captain plans to enter a shallow harbor during a quarter-moon phase. What should she expect?
options: A smaller difference between high and low tide than at full moon
No high tide at all that day
The largest tides of the whole month, much higher than usual
Tides that come only once that day
questions.why: Quarter moons bring neap tides, which are weaker, so the difference between high and low water is smaller.

wrong.B: Most coasts still have two high tides a day.
wrong.C: The largest tides are spring tides at new and full moon.
wrong.D: Neap tides change the size of tides, not how often they come.

questions.stem: Why does the author compare the Bay of Fundy with Saudi Arabia's Red Sea coast?
options: To argue that Canada has better beaches
To explain why the Red Sea is salty
To show how greatly tidal range varies from place to place
To describe two good places for tidal power
questions.why: The author places a range of about 16 meters beside a range under one meter to show how much tides vary.

wrong.D: Tidal power is not linked to these two places.

HIGH.prompt: Some people say the Moon is more important to life on the coast than the Sun. Do you agree or disagree? Support your position with evidence from the article.
checklist: I supported it with at least two pieces of evidence from the article.
I explained how my evidence supports my position.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I agree that the Moon is more important to life on the coast than the Sun. The article explains that the Moon's gravitational pull is the main cause of tides, creating the bulges of water that produce high and low tide every day, while the Sun's pull is less than half as strong because it is so far away. Whether the Moon is aligned with the Sun or pulling at a nearly perpendicular angle also decides whether a coast gets an extra-large spring tide or a weaker neap tide, showing how closely coastal life follows the Moon's phase. Since sailors depend on predicted tides for navigation and some countries use the movement of tides as a renewable source of electricity, the Moon's daily influence clearly outweighs the Sun's.
